questions.question: What is the difference between for, while, and do-while loops in Java?
questions.title: for vs while vs do-while Loops in Java
questions.direct_answer: **`for` loops** are used when you know the number of iterations in advance. **`while` loops** run as long as a condition is true, checked before each iteration. **`do-while` loops** always execute at least once because the condition is checked after the loop body.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic understanding of loop constructs and when to pick each one
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that do-while guarantees at least one execution — a key differentiator
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a real-world use case for each: for (iterating an array), while (reading input until EOF), do-while (show menu at least once)

sections.title: Three Loop Constructs
Loop Comparison
sections.content:
| Aspect | for | while | do-while |
|---|---|---|---|
| When to use | Known iterations | Unknown iterations, condition-driven | Must run at least once |
| Condition check | Before loop | Before loop | After loop body |
| Min executions | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| Common use case | Array traversal | Reading until EOF | Menu-driven programs |

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: So the key difference is when the condition is checked. Both `for` and `while` check the condition before executing the body, so they might run zero times if the condition is false from the start. `do-while` checks after the body, so it's guaranteed to execute at least once. When to use which: use `for` when you know how many times to iterate, like going through an array. Use `while` when you're looping based on a condition that might be false initially. Use `do-while` for things like menus where you need to show options to the user at least once before checking if they want to exit.

questions.question: What is the difference between break, continue, and return in Java?
questions.title: break vs continue vs return in Java Loops
questions.direct_answer: **`break`** exits the loop entirely. **`continue`** skips the current iteration and moves to the next. **`return`** exits the entire method — not just the loop. These three statements control flow in fundamentally different ways.

interviewer_intent.testing: Precise understanding of loop control — a common source of bugs for freshers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking break exits the method, or confusing continue with break
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention labeled break/continue for nested loops, and when return from inside a loop is useful (early exit pattern)

sections.title: break, continue, and return
Key Points
sections.content:
- `break` — exits the **current loop** (or switch case); execution continues after the loop
- `continue` — skips **current iteration**; loop condition is re-evaluated
- `return` — exits the **entire method**; control returns to the caller
- Labeled `break outerLoop;` can break out of **nested loops** (useful but use sparingly)
- `continue` cannot be used in switch statements (only loops)
- In switch, `break` prevents fall-through to the next case

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: So these three have different scopes of effect. `continue` is the smallest — it just skips the rest of the current loop iteration and jumps to the next one. `break` is bigger — it stops the entire loop and execution continues with whatever comes after the loop. And `return` is the biggest — it exits the whole method entirely. A common use case for return inside a loop is an early-exit search pattern: you loop through an array, and the moment you find what you're looking for, you return it — no need to keep looping.

questions.question: What is the enhanced for-each loop in Java and when should you use it?
questions.title: Enhanced for-each Loop in Java
questions.direct_answer: The **enhanced for-each loop** (introduced in Java 5) iterates over arrays and any `Iterable` collection without needing an index counter. It's cleaner and less error-prone than a traditional for loop when you only need to read elements and don't need the index.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate writes idiomatic modern Java vs C-style for loops for everything
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using for-each when you need the index or when you need to modify the array — for-each doesn't give you the index and won't modify the source array
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain that for-each calls iterator() behind the scenes for collections, and that you can't remove elements during iteration (use Iterator.remove() or removeIf() instead)

sections.title: for-each Syntax and Behavior
Key Points
sections.content:
- Works on arrays and any class implementing `Iterable<T>`
- Compiler converts it to an Iterator-based loop for collections
- Cannot remove elements during iteration (causes `ConcurrentModificationException`)
- Assigning to loop variable doesn't modify the source array (`num = 5` won't change the array)
- Use `Iterator` explicitly if you need `remove()` during iteration
- For modifying elements: use traditional for loop for arrays, `List.set()` etc. for collections

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: The enhanced for-each was introduced in Java 5 as a cleaner way to iterate over arrays and collections when you just need to read the elements. The syntax is `for (Type element : collection)` and it's much easier to read than managing an index variable yourself. The main limitation is that you don't get the index — so if you need to know the position of each element, or if you need to modify elements, you should use a regular for loop instead. Another gotcha is that you can't remove elements from a collection while iterating with for-each — that will throw a ConcurrentModificationException.

questions.question: What is the difference between if-else and switch in Java, and when should you prefer switch?
questions.title: if-else vs switch Statement in Java
questions.direct_answer: **`if-else`** can test any boolean expression including ranges and complex conditions. **`switch`** tests a single variable against discrete values and is more readable for multiple fixed choices. Java 14+ added **switch expressions** with arrow syntax that eliminate fall-through issues.

interviewer_intent.testing: Design judgment — when to use each construct, not just syntax knowledge
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing about switch fall-through (forgetting break causes execution to continue to next case) or the newer switch expression syntax
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention switch can work with String (Java 7+), enum, and the new arrow syntax in Java 14+ that makes switch safer and more expressive

sections.title: if-else vs switch
if-else vs switch
sections.content:
| Aspect | if-else | switch |
|---|---|---|
| Condition type | Any boolean expression | Equality against discrete values |
| Range checks | Yes (`x > 5 && x < 10`) | No |
| Data types | Any | int, char, String, enum (not long/float) |
| Fall-through | N/A | Yes (traditional), No (arrow syntax) |
| Readability | Good for 1-3 conditions | Better for 4+ discrete values |

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: So if-else is more flexible — you can test any condition including ranges, complex expressions, or null checks. Switch is better when you're comparing a single variable against several specific values, like days of the week or status codes — it's more readable in those cases. The classic gotcha with traditional switch is fall-through: if you forget a break statement, execution runs into the next case. Java 14 introduced switch expressions with arrow syntax that fixed this — no more accidental fall-through. Switch works with int, char, String, and enums, but notably not with long or float.

questions.question: What will the following code output and why? A switch case with a missing break statement.
questions.title: Switch Fall-Through Gotcha in Java
questions.direct_answer: Without `break`, a switch statement **falls through** to the next case and executes it too, regardless of whether that case matched. This is a classic Java gotcha that causes multiple cases to execute from the first matching case downward.

interviewer_intent.testing: Attention to detail and understanding of switch semantics — interviewers love this gotcha
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Assuming each case executes independently like if-else branches
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that fall-through can sometimes be intentional (like grouping multiple cases), and that Java 14+ arrow switch syntax eliminates this problem entirely

sections.title: Switch Fall-Through Explained
sections.content:
```java
int x = 2;
switch (x) {
    case 1:
        System.out.println("one");
    case 2:
        System.out.println("two");   // matches here
    case 3:
        System.out.println("three"); // falls through!
    default:
        System.out.println("default"); // falls through!
}
// Output: two  three  default
```

Execution starts at the matching case (`case 2`) and then **falls through every subsequent case** until it hits a `break` or the end of the switch block.

**Intentional fall-through** (valid use case):
```java
case "SAT":
case "SUN":
    System.out.println("Weekend"); // both days share same code
    break;
```

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- Without `break`, execution continues into the next case regardless of its value
- `default` also participates in fall-through if no break precedes it
- Intentional fall-through (multiple cases, same action) is a legitimate pattern
- Java 14+ **arrow syntax** (`case 2 -> ...`) eliminates fall-through entirely
- The `@SuppressWarnings("fallthrough")` annotation documents intentional fall-through
- This is one of the most common Java interview gotcha questions

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: This is a classic fall-through scenario. When switch matches case 2, it prints 'two' — but because there's no break, it doesn't stop. It falls through into case 3 and prints 'three', then falls through into default and prints 'default'. So the output is: two, three, default — all three lines. The fix is to add a break at the end of each case. That said, fall-through can be intentional — if you want Saturday and Sunday to execute the same code, you can stack `case "SAT":` and `case "SUN":` with no break between them. Java 14's new arrow switch syntax solves this entirely because it never falls through.

beats.text: Switch fall-through means execution continues into the next case after a match if there's no break statement. The switch jumps to the matching case then keeps executing all subsequent cases until it hits a break or the end of the block.

Fall-through was inherited from C and can be useful intentionally — stacking multiple cases to share the same code block. But it causes bugs when forgotten, so Java 14 introduced arrow syntax that never falls through.

With break at the end of each case: only the matching case runs.
Intentional use: case SAT: case SUN: share code by stacking with no break between.

Candidates miss that default also falls through if no break precedes it. Java 14 arrow syntax — case 2 -> ... — eliminates fall-through entirely.

questions.question: How do nested loops work in Java and what are the common pitfalls?
questions.title: Nested Loops in Java — Patterns and Pitfalls
questions.direct_answer: **Nested loops** are loops inside loops. The inner loop completes all its iterations for each iteration of the outer loop. The main pitfall is **performance**: if the outer loop runs N times and inner M times, total iterations are N×M — this can be prohibitively slow for large inputs (O(n²) complexity).

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic algorithmic thinking and awareness of time complexity — important even for freshers
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not realizing that nested loops are O(n²) and can be very slow, or misunderstanding which break exits which loop
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention labeled break for nested loops, and that many O(n²) solutions can be optimized to O(n log n) or O(n) with better data structures

sections.title: Nested Loops and Complexity
Key Points
sections.content:
- Total iterations = outer iterations × inner iterations (O(n²) for equal sizes)
- Plain `break` exits only the innermost loop
- **Labeled break** (`break outerLabel;`) exits a specific outer loop
- Nested loops often signal an opportunity for optimization in interviews
- Common uses: matrix traversal, comparing all pairs, generating patterns
- Three levels of nesting (O(n³)) is usually a warning sign for performance

sections.title: How to Answer in an Interview
sections.content: Nested loops run the inner loop fully for every iteration of the outer loop. So if both loops run n times, you get n-squared total iterations — that's O(n²) complexity. The gotcha with break is that it only exits the innermost loop, not all the loops. If you need to exit a nested loop from inside, Java supports labeled break where you put a label before the outer loop and use `break labelName` to jump out of it entirely. In interviews, if you write a nested loop solution, it's good to acknowledge the O(n²) cost and mention if there's a way to optimize it.

beats.text: A nested loop is a loop inside another loop. For each iteration of the outer loop, the inner loop runs completely. So if the outer runs N times and the inner M times, total iterations are N times M.

Some problems naturally require visiting every pair of elements — like matrix traversal or brute-force search. Nested loops are the straightforward tool for that, but they come with a performance cost that grows fast.

break only exits the innermost loop — use labeled break to exit an outer loop.
Three levels of nesting means O(n cubed) — usually a red flag for performance.

beats.text: In a Java 17 console app, a 3x3 multiplication table uses nested loops: outer i from 1 to 3, inner j from 1 to 3 — 9 total iterations. To break out of both loops at once, label the outer loop: outer: for(...) { for(...) { if(condition) break outer; } }. Non-obvious: a plain break inside only exits the inner loop, and the outer loop keeps running.

production trap: O(n squared) feels fine for small n but becomes unusable for thousands of elements — always consider if a HashMap or sorting can reduce it.
